tier_reason: The README (last updated 2026-09-10) includes rows for the capnp 0.27.0, flatbuffers 25.12.19, prost 0.14.4/protobuf and rmp-serde/msgpacker/zerompk crates. It states the compiler (rustc 1.100.0-nightly, LLVM 23.1.1) and the CPU (AMD EPYC 9V74). The flags are in the public code: tools/bencher/src/main.rs runs `cargo bench` with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', and Cargo.toml sets [profile.bench] lto = true. The benchmark code is benches/bench.rs with src/bench_rkyv.rs, src/bench_flatbuffers.rs, src/bench_capnp.rs, src/bench_prost.rs and src/bench_rmp_serde.rs.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On the 'log' dataset (page run 2026-09-10), rkyv serializes in 178.87 µs, against 763.63 µs for FlatBuffers (~4.3x, derived from page data), 480.15 µs for Cap'n Proto (~2.7x, derived from page data), 731.23 µs for prost encode and 1.3179 ms for rmp-serde. Unvalidated zero-copy access takes 1.0907 ns against 2.1807 ns for FlatBuffers. Unvalidated read takes 8.3309 µs against 42.209 µs for FlatBuffers; the record's '8.33 µs deserialize' was this read figure. rkyv's full unvalidated deserialize takes 1.2188 ms, against 2.6802 ms for prost decode and 2.3829 ms for rmp-serde. rkyv serialize also beats all four baselines on the other datasets: mesh 141.74 µs (FlatBuffers 371.26 µs), minecraft_savedata 212.50 µs (Cap'n Proto 392.46 µs) and mk48 798.81 µs (Cap'n Proto 2.1159 ms). It is not the fastest Rust crate overall. Its serialize speed relative to the best crate is 54.13% (log), 100% (mesh), 38.61% (minecraft_savedata) and 64.85% (mk48). bitcode leads on log and minecraft_savedata.
corrections.workload: Criterion benchmarks in rust_serialization_benchmark on four Rust datasets: log (HTTP request logs), mesh (triangle mesh), minecraft_savedata (Minecraft player saves) and mk48 (mk48.io game updates). They measure serialize, deserialize, zero-copy access, read and update times, plus encoded size and compressed size. The baselines are Rust crates: capnp 0.27.0, flatbuffers 25.12.19, prost 0.14.4, protobuf 3.7.2 and 4.36.1, rmp-serde 1.3.1, msgpacker 0.7.1 and zerompk 0.8.0.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.100.0-nightly (a36d05efa 2026-09-09), LLVM 23.1.1. `cargo bench` runs with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' (tools/bencher/src/main.rs). Cargo.toml sets [profile.bench] lto = true; opt-level 3 is inherited from release. Criterion harness.
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 4 vCPUs (2 cores x 2 threads), on a Microsoft Hyper-V VM (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner), x86_64
corrections.caveats: The benchmark repo (rust_serialization_benchmark) is maintained by rkyv's author (djkoloski) with other volunteers, so it is not fully independent. It is public, reproducible and covers about 27 crates. The baselines are the Rust implementations of each format (capnp, flatbuffers, prost/protobuf, rmp-serde crates), not the C++ reference libraries. CI regenerates the README on a shared cloud VM, so the figures drift between runs; these are from the 2026-09-10 run. The fastest access, read and deserialize figures use unsafe unvalidated APIs. Validated access on log costs 274.32 µs, against 2.1354 ms for FlatBuffers validated. The original 'rkyv is faster than...' blog post domain is dead or redirected. Relative performance varies by dataset.

notes: I confirmed Tier A. The log, mesh, minecraft_savedata and mk48 figures all match the auto-generated README tables. I fixed one mislabel: the '8.33 µs vs 42.2 µs deserialize' pair is the zero-copy Read column, and the real unvalidated deserialize figure is 1.2188 ms. Metadata checked: MIT, 4,362 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-25.

tier_reason: These are first-party numbers. greenpack's author added greenpack to his own 8-star fork of alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks in 2017, and the 1.6k-star upstream suite has never included greenpack. The code is public (serialization_benchmarks_test.go), but no flags and no CPU model are given (only '3.1 GHz Intel Core i7'). The Go version is uncertain. The fork is not a well-known independent suite, so B does not apply.

corrections.claimed_speedup: This claim holds for writes only. GreenPackMarshal takes 129 ns/op with 0 B/op, against 152 ns/op with 64 B/op for GogoprotobufMarshal (~15% faster, derived from page data). It is also faster than golang/protobuf (GoprotobufMarshal, 500 ns/op), DeDiS/protobuf (ProtobufMarshal, reflection-based, 936 ns/op), FlatBuffers Go (379 ns/op) and Cap'n Proto via glycerine/go-capnproto (498 ns/op). ZebraPack, by the same author, is faster at 120 ns/op. The README's '6% faster reads' does not measure greenpack. It rests on GreenPackUnmarshal (224 ns/op) against GogoprotobufUnmarshal (240 ns/op), but BenchmarkGreenPackUnmarshal calls ZebraPack's ZMarshalMsg/ZUnmarshalMsg, not GreenUnmarshalMsg. That row is therefore a second run of BenchmarkZebraPackUnmarshal, which measured 236 ns/op in the same run.
corrections.baseline: Protocol Buffers (Go implementations: gogo/protobuf gogofaster, golang/protobuf, DeDiS/protobuf); FlatBuffers Go and Cap'n Proto Go are also in the table
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The README header says 'Go 1.8beta2'. The August 2017 commit that added greenpack (de65278) replaced the result tables but left that header from the January 2017 run unchanged, so the Go version of the greenpack run is unconfirmed. The command is go test -bench='.*' ./ and no other flags are given.
corrections.hardware: 3.1 GHz Intel Core i7 (MacBook Pro 13"); no CPU model number stated
corrections.caveats: These are first-party numbers: greenpack's author ran them in his own fork (glycerine/go_serialization_benchmarks, 8 stars, last commit 2017-08-05). The upstream alecthomas suite does not include greenpack. The read comparison is invalid because of a copy-paste bug: BenchmarkGreenPackUnmarshal uses ZebraPack's generated ZMarshalMsg/ZUnmarshalMsg. The throughput columns confirm this: the 'greenpack' unmarshal payload is ~59 bytes, the same as ZebraPack's, while greenpack marshal emits ~142 bytes. Only the write result measures greenpack. The margins are small next to run-to-run noise: the earlier run had ZebraPackUnmarshal at 227 ns/op and Gogoprotobuf at 232 ns/op. Hardware and Go version (2017, Go 1.8-era) are dated. The only baselines are Go protobuf implementations, not C++ protobuf. greenpack itself is still maintained, with a last commit on 2026-01-23.

notes: I downgraded from B to C because the benchmark is first-party and the README's read claim does not hold. BenchmarkGreenPackUnmarshal decodes with ZebraPack's methods, so only the write result (129 vs 152 ns/op against gogoprotobuf) measures greenpack. The record's '936 ns/op Protobuf' figure is DeDiS/protobuf; golang/protobuf is 500 ns/op. Metadata checked: MIT, 115 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-01-23 (active).

tier_reason: This is the project author's own benchmark (sourcemeta/json-size-benchmark, whose Dockerfile pins the implementation versions). The arXiv write-ups 2211.12799 and 2201.03051 are preprints with no journal reference, so they are not peer-reviewed; an MSc dissertation is not a peer-reviewed paper either. No compiler, flags or CPU are given, which matters little for a size benchmark, but those are the tier rules. That makes it first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: This is a size result only; nothing is claimed about speed. In all 27 documents, JSON BinPack (schema-driven) produced the smallest or tied-smallest uncompressed encoding. The comparison covered Protocol Buffers (Python protobuf 3.12.4), FlatBuffers (flatc 1.12.0), Cap'n Proto 0.7.0 (binary and packed), MessagePack (Python msgpack 1.0.0), Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers and JSON. On four documents it ties with Avro and/or Protocol Buffers. Example: the ESLint configuration encodes to 64 bytes against 1,141 bytes of JSON (~94.4% smaller, derived from page data). Across the 27 documents the median reduction against JSON is ~86.8% and the mean ~78.8% (derived from page data; arXiv 2211.12799 reports 86.7% and 78.7%). The schema-driven uncompressed output is smaller than JSON compressed with GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 or LZMA -9 in all 27 documents (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Encoded size of 27 real-world JSON documents from SchemaStore, measured uncompressed and after GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 and LZMA -9. There is one document per JSON Taxonomy class (tier x type x redundancy x structure), and each is encoded with JSON BinPack (schema-driven and schema-less) and 13 other formats. JSON BinPack was run through the TypeScript proof of concept (npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x), not the C++ code in this repo.
corrections.caveats: The win is size, not speed. The README concedes runtime efficiency and recommends FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto for extreme runtime efficiency or zero-copy use. The benchmark covers 27 documents; the '400+ SchemaStore documents' figure comes from arXiv 2201.03051, which does not include JSON BinPack. The benchmark ran the archived TypeScript proof of concept (jviotti/jsonbinpack-poc, npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x, February 2022; the page lists 1.1.1 and the Dockerfile installs 1.1.2). The current C++ implementation in this repo is not measured, and the wire format may have changed since. The benchmark is first-party, by the project's author, and the arXiv write-ups are preprints, not peer-reviewed. The README says the MSc dissertation won the 2022 CAR Hoare Prizes. The competitors are older versions (protobuf 3.12.4, flatc 1.12.0, Cap'n Proto 0.7.0). No compiler or hardware is stated, which is irrelevant for byte counts. The license is dual: AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial.

notes: This is a scope rejection (not-faster): every number checks out, but JSON BinPack's claim is encoded size, and its own README hands runtime speed to FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto. Under the keep-flagged-entries policy, it could stay with this shortcoming, tier C. Another shortcoming: the benchmark measured the archived TypeScript proof of concept, not this C++ repo. Metadata checked: GitHub shows the license as NOASSERTION, and the LICENSE file gives AGPL-3.0-or-later or commercial (OSI-approved, copyable). 164 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-23.
